R. 3.6 We recommend that all boys who receive pubertal induction therapy should have a structured endocrine assessment at baseline and at follow-up. Rationale Regular clinical follow-up is generally performed every 3–6 months to assess the effectiveness of testosterone therapy by assessing pubertal and skeletal maturation and height velocity. In the guidelines for adults on testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), monitoring is recommended and standardised ( , ). There is clear evidence that systematic monitoring in adolescents on testosterone is performed to a variable extent ( ) and it is possible that this variation is due to the wide range of conditions that necessitate TRT in adolescents. Recently, monitoring schemes designed to assess the effectiveness as well as safety of TRT have been proposed ( ). With greater knowledge of a wider range of effects of testosterone and the advent of several newer forms of testosterone replacement, the need for careful monitoring is becoming greater. A structured assessment can also be used to screen for adverse effects as well as titrate replacement. It should include the assessment of adverse signs such as local reactions, gynaecomastia, priapism, increased haematocrit, deranged liver function and inappropriate behavioural changes. highlights the advantages and disadvantages of specific preparations and further details can also be found in recent publications ( , , ). While there is no evidence that dose titration against a marker such as a haematocrit is necessary for pubertal induction, the regular assessment of haematocrit would be advisable, especially as the adolescent reaches a steady adult replacement dose ( ). The care pathway can also ensure age-appropriate explanations and discussions about both endocrine and reproductive testicular functions with the appropriate experts in the multidisciplinary team. With increasing maturity, these discussions may cover issues regarding sexual function and fertility including biological fathering and other modes of fathering. Physiological variations in steroid metabolism as well as androgen sensitivity when combined with the wide range of preparations that are available increase the likelihood of inter-individual differences in how boys will respond to replacement therapy and there is a need for clinically relevant markers of androgen action. R. 3.7 We suggest adjusting the puberty induction treatment or changing the route of administration in case of relevant adverse effects/complications. Rationale The occurrence of relevant adverse effects is rare with testosterone ( ). For injectable forms of TRT, priapism has rarely been reported. Testosterone undecanoate, the long-acting preparation, should not be used for induction of puberty or progression through the early stages of puberty, as it is likely to advance bone age too rapidly with a potential for truncating final height. When ingested orally, testosterone is absorbed well from the gut but is effectively metabolised and inactivated in the liver before it reaches the target organs (‘first pass-effect’). Testosterone induces liver enzymes that are responsible for its own metabolism. Testosterone gel provides a possibility for more physiologic serum testosterone levels and it can closely mimic natural diurnal variation in testosterone concentrations. It has only minor systemic side effects. However, published data on transdermal testosterone in pubertal induction are scarce. In many countries, testosterone formulations are not licenced for the induction of puberty. Transdermal gels are available in different formulations: 1% testosterone strength and the metered-dose gel formulation of 2% or 2.5% testosterone strength. Topical testosterone has been repeatedly reported to cause undesirable exogenous testosterone exposure through passive transfer to members of the patients’ household ( ). Due to the alcoholic enhancer used and the occlusive nature of the systems, the application is associated with skin irritation in up to 60% of the subjects. It should be remembered that 50% of all adolescents develop gynaecomastia which typically presents in early puberty and lasts for 6–12 months. Gynaecomastia occurs in up to a third of patients on gonadotropins ( ) or testosterone ( ) and usually (although not invariably) occurs during supraphysiological replacement doses. The risk and severity of gynaecomastia can be reversed by adjusting the dosage. It should be remembered that 50% of all adolescents develop gynaecomastia which typically presents in early puberty and lasts for 6–12 months. Similarly to physiological puberty, the most likely cause of gynaecomastia during TRT is a relative imbalance between oestrogen and androgen levels in the serum or at the tissue level ( ). During the early proliferative phase, manifested clinically as breast pain and tenderness, medical therapy may be attempted ( ). Medical treatment of gynaecomastia aims to correct the oestrogen–androgen imbalance by three possible pathways: (i) blocking the effects of oestrogens on the breast (e.g. clomiphene, tamoxifen, raloxifene), (ii) administering androgens (e.g. danazol or DHT) and (iii) inhibiting oestrogen production (e.g. anastrozole, testolactone). Almost all data dealing with these treatments are based on uncontrolled studies, and in addition, the evaluation of their efficacy is further complicated by the fact that gynaecomastia may resolve spontaneously ( , ). It must be noted that none of these therapies are approved for the treatment of gynaecomastia. It seems to be reasonable to try a 3 months trial in selected cases of recent-onset gynaecomastia ( ) because it offers rapid relief from pain, regardless of the magnitude of the response. If the gynaecomastia has been present for >1 year, it is unlikely to regress substantially, either spontaneously or with medical therapy, because fibrotic tissue is usually present. In such circumstances, surgical s.c. mastectomy, ultrasound-assisted liposuction and suction-assisted lipectomy are the best options for cosmetic improvement of Tanner stage III and above ( , ). R 3.9 Treatment in patients with a late diagnosis, without pubertal development or for whom the pubertal development has come to a halt, should be individualised. Rationale Patients who come to diagnosis at a later age, towards the late teenage years or as young adults, may have no pubertal development or a spontaneous start of puberty but a slow or no pubertal progress. This is often the case in young men with Klinefelter syndrome and can be the case in individuals with 45,X/46,XY, gonadal dysgenesis or androgen insensitivity. Adult endocrinologists often see patients with CHH in late adolescence or early adulthood with the main complaint of lack of pubertal development ( ). In such cases, the therapeutic approach is often more incisive than for younger patients, involving higher initial testosterone doses than those used by paediatric endocrinologists (200–250mg testosterone enanthate monthly, then every 2–3 weeks) to induce more rapid virilisation ( ). Pubertal induction in patients with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism Introduction HH is caused by congenital or acquired defects of the hypothalamic and/or pituitary compartment of the HPG axis. CHH forms can be isolated, part of an overlapping syndrome (such as CHARGE) or part of combined pituitary hormone deficits. Kallmann syndrome is associated with hypo- or anosmia. All these forms have strong genetic backgrounds ( ). Acquired forms of HH, mainly associated with other pituitary hormone deficits, are usually the results of neoplastic, metabolic, immune, infectious, infiltrative, inflammatory or iatrogenic causes affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary region. HH can also be related to functional causes, which are usually characterised by a reversible negative effect on the HPG axis activation/functionality. These include chronic and/or inflammatory systemic illness, malnutrition (e.g. anorexia nervosa), extreme exercise or stressful conditions and opioid use. Pubertal induction has to be considered in all cases with permanent HH after the diagnostic procedure has been carefully followed. The goals of the therapy for pubertal induction in male and female HH are not different from the ones reported for primary hypogonadism, although in this specific cohort of patients, the possibility of future fertility can be considered and, in males, specific treatment regimens can allow for the maturation of testes ( , ). Briefly, the main goals will be the attainment of optimal masculinisation/feminisation and secondary sexual characteristics; the achievement of pubertal growth and an optimal target height; the prevention of osteoporosis by accruing normal bone mass and mineralisation; to allow for a normal psychosocial development; and in certain cases, to gain fertility ( , , , ). However, it should be pointed out that the main differential diagnosis of CHH is CDGP. It is a more common situation and also more frequent in boys compared to girls. Timing of puberty induction In principle, the timing for pubertal induction in patients with a diagnosis of permanent HH does not differ from what has been recommended for boys and girls with hypogonadism. However, it should be pointed out that the main differential diagnosis of CHH is CDGP. It is a more common situation and also more frequent in boys compared to girls. This differential diagnosis is one of the greatest challenges for the clinician evaluating a pubertal delay ( ). Unfortunately, to date, we do not have specific indicators that allow for a clear distinction between these two clinical conditions although a history of micropenis, bilateral cryptorchism, midline defect, hypo/anosmia, deafness or renal anomalies should raise the suspicion of CHH. For this reason, in patients with pubertal delay and uncertainty regarding the diagnosis of CHH or CDGP, it may sometime be necessary to delay the initiation of induction even beyond 14 years. Nonetheless, the decision must always be made according to the clinical situation in each individual case and in concern with the patient him/herself and his/her parents ( , , ). Treatment approach and monitoring Recommendations regarding treatment approach and monitoring for puberty induction in girls (R 2.1–2.9) apply equally to those with HH. Pubertal induction in girls with HH using gonadotropins has not been described, although gonadotropin–ovulation–induction is a standard fertility treatment in adult life. R 4.1 We suggest discussing two treatment options for pubertal induction in boys with secondary hypogonadism: testosterone or gonadotropins. See for the so far reported different treatment options using gonadotrophins. (+OOO) Rationale Pubertal induction in a boy can be carried out through two different possible approaches: the use of testosterone analogues similar to the treatment of primary hypogonadism or the use of exogenous gonadotropins. Preparations, doses and aim of the two possible treatments are indicated in R 3.1–3.5 and and . Monitoring of patients with HH undergoing gonadotropin treatment does not differ from the recommendation for pubertal induction with testosterone (see R 3.5–R 3.8). To date only a few randomised studies have been published comparing these different treatment strategies and the patients recruited in these studies are often quite heterogeneous. It is therefore difficult to conclude which treatment strategy is more effective or preferred ( ). A systematic review provided no firm evidence for an optimal induction approach (see section on Systematic literature review) ( , , , ). The two options, testosterone or gonadotropins ( ), should be presented and discussed with the patient and his parents, also considering the availability of the different treatment options in the patient’s country of residence. The most common treatment for pubertal induction in males with HH involves, as for primary hypogonadism, the use of i.m. injection of testosterone esters (enanthate, propionate or cypionate) ( , , , , ). Although effective in inducing pubertal signs and symptoms, testosterone formulations neither stimulate testicular growth nor will they induce spermatogenesis. It is still unclear whether testosterone therapy for pubertal induction hinders future testis development or likelihood of spermatogenesis if gonadotropins are used in adulthood ( , ). Alternatively, a potential testicular development and fertility in males with HH can be achieved with puberty induction through the use of gonadotropins ( , , , ). This might offer adolescent patients a significant psychological reassurance and may also enhance their self-confidence ( , ). On the other hand, although this has to be verified and demonstrated, it might also allow for the early identification of potential ‘poor responders’ (i.e. patients with severe oligozoospermia and a total sperm count <5 millions/mL) and thus give them the opportunity to consider a preventive and prophylactic sperm cryopreservation for future use in case of a worse spermatic response in adulthood. Different treatment protocols with gonadotropins can be used to induce puberty in adolescent males with HH: exogenous hCG alone or in combination with recombinant FSH ( , , , , ). However, consistent evidence suggests that the combination therapy with recombinant FSH (rFSH)/hCG is significantly more effective than hCG alone both for inducing spermatogenesis and increasing testicular volume. Furthermore, some evidence suggests that a pre-treatment with rFSH followed by the combination with hCG or GnRH is even more effective in optimising the Sertoli cell maturation and is able to induce spermatogenesis even in extremely small testes, and cryopreservation of sperm subsequently allows for enhancing the future fertility of these patients ( , , , ). Indeed, this approach mimics the physiological elevation of FSH during spontaneous pubertal development. Furthermore, some evidence suggests that a pre-treatment with rFSH followed by the combination with hCG or GnRH is even more effective in optimising the Sertoli cell maturation and is able to induce spermatogenesis even in extremely small testes, and cryopreservation of sperm subsequently allows for enhancing the future fertility of these patients ( , , , ). Indeed, this approach mimics the physiological elevation of FSH during spontaneous pubertal development. Treatment with gonadotropins, whatever the protocol used, requires multiple weekly injections, although s.c. injections can be given. This aspect should be discussed with the patient and parents before the final decision. R 4.2 We suggest considering switching gonadotropins to testosterone in boys with HH after pubertal induction. Rationale If pubertal induction is made by the administration of rFSH and hCG in order to mimic physiology, we recommend switching to testosterone treatment in boys with HH after the completion of pubertal induction. Possible spermatogenesis should be considered. Although there is not enough evidence to recommend one treatment before the other, there are theoretical arguments based on the limited knowledge available on testis and Sertoli cell maturation with regard to fertility. During early puberty, the proliferation of immature Sertoli cells occurs under the stimulus of FSH. Hence, treatment with FSH stimulates the proliferation of immature Sertoli cells and spermatogonia ( , , ). On the other hand, testosterone induces the differentiation of Sertoli cells via androgen receptor which begins to be expressed after the first 5 years of life ( , ). The combination of rFSH and hCG therapy for 6–24 months results in testicular growth in almost all and spermatogenesis in 80–95% of patients without undescended testes ( , , , , ). The use of hCG without FSH priming could, therefore, in theory, cause premature differentiation of the pool of Sertoli and germ cells, thereby diminishing the chance of proliferation leading to lower fertility potential in adulthood. The shift from FSH/hCG therapy to testosterone should occur after sperm analysis, and in the case of sufficient sperm in the ejaculate, sperm cryopreservation (banking) should be considered, particularly in severe oligospermia. The reason behind this is that even if repeated gonadotropin treatment has been reported to induce quicker initiation of spermatogenesis ( , ), it is not certain. In cases with azoospermia, which then appear as ‘poor responders’ to gonadotropin stimulation, testicular sperm extraction (TESE) procedure might be considered, however, with uncertain outcome, before switching to TRT, especially in patients who are old and mature enough for this. Furthermore, since ‘reversal’ of CHH has been described ( ) in 5–20% of patients with CHH, a brief therapy withdrawal (i.e. 4 months) after the conclusion of pubertal induction with gonadotropins and before the start of TRT might be considered in order to verify a spontaneous recovery of the HPG axis. Puberty induction in Klinefelter Introduction Klinefelter syndrome is the most common cause of congenital male hypogonadism. However, boys with this syndrome typically enter puberty at a normal age. With advancing adolescent age, the gonadal dysfunction becomes more marked and may be associated with a failure to progress in puberty ( ). The diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome affecting 1:600 men is often overlooked ( , ) with less than 10% diagnosed before puberty, probably due to the variable and sometimes subtle phenotype, especially in the mosaic forms. During or after puberty, boys with Klinefelter syndrome typically present with gynaecomastia and they have elevated FSH and low testosterone levels, although testosterone can also be at the lower end of the normal range with elevated LH ( , ). Patients have an increased incidence of cryptorchidism. In puberty, the testes grow initially and then regress, and in adulthood, testes are small and firm. There is a wide spectrum of the phenotype, many are never even diagnosed while some can have psychosocial difficulties and learning disabilities. The diagnosis is confirmed by karyotyping. We place a high value on the recommendation to treat adult patients with Klinefelter syndrome and low testosterone levels as well as accompanying symptoms of androgen deficiency with an adequately dosed testosterone replacement ( ). Timing of puberty induction The general recommendations as formulated under R 3.1 and 3.3 (in whom to consider pubertal induction) apply to Klinefelter syndrome, although the most common situation is a normal start of puberty followed by a slow progression of puberty with small testes and development of gynaecomastia. Treatment approach and monitoring With regard to the timing of puberty, an individual prediction of pubertal onset for patients with Klinefelter syndrome can be estimated from the parents’ pubertal history. Whether early testosterone replacement, when LH starts to rise above normal levels (>+2 s.d. ), should be started is still not clear. Some advocate for early treatment as soon as LH starts to rise in

(in whom to consider pubertal induction) apply to Klinefelter syndrome, although the most common situation is a normal start of puberty followed by a slow progression of puberty with small testes and development of gynaecomastia. Treatment approach and monitoring With regard to the timing of puberty, an individual prediction of pubertal onset for patients with Klinefelter syndrome can be estimated from the parents’ pubertal history. Whether early testosterone replacement, when LH starts to rise above normal levels (>+2 s.d. ), should be started is still not clear. Some advocate for early treatment as soon as LH starts to rise in order to prevent the adverse body composition, osteopenia/osteoporosis, impaired physical and psychological development, educational achievements and social integration which are commonly observed in the untreated newly diagnosed young adult ( , , , , ). However, others think that testosterone supplementation should be postponed until testosterone levels fall below the normal range (<−2 s.d. ) ( ). Some in the expert group advocated for aiming at securing sperm for cryopreservation before starting testosterone supplementation, while others, in the absence of scientific evidence for such an approach, advocated for commencing testosterone supplementation as soon as LH starts to rise. The recommendations regarding treatment and monitoring R 3.5–3.9 apply equally to Klinefelter. R. 5.3 We suggest performing sperm analysis if physically and mentally possible before the start of testosterone treatment in boys with Klinefelter Syndrome and spontaneous start of puberty. Rationale Randomised–controlled trials are needed to elucidate the influence of testosterone replacement therapy on pubertal development and spermatogenesis in patients with Klinefelter Syndrome. There are also no randomised–controlled trials evaluating the possible deleterious impact of testosterone treatment on successful sperm retrieval or its possible effects on reproductive outcomes in men with Klinefelter Syndrome. Testosterone preparations may theoretically suppress any remaining spermatogenesis if the endogenous LH drive is reduced; however, this has not been shown in clinical trials. Some advocate for assessing fertility status before the start of testosterone supplementation, while others do not. Therefore, individual decisions should be made until more evidence is gathered. In those patients who have no spermatozoa in their ejaculate, fertility preservation can be attempted through TESE. According to a recent literature review, spermatozoa can be found by TESE in up to half of the patients with Klinefelter syndrome aged 16–30 years old, of whom many had been treated with testosterone ( ), although real-life studies report much lower values ( ). Therefore, a TESE procedure for fertility preservation should not be performed in Klinefelter syndrome patients younger than 16 years and it can be postponed at least until the age of 30 since no significant differences were observed in TESE outcome in this age interval. The use of hCG or anti-oestrogens (aromatase inhibitors or selective oestrogen receptor modulators) on compassionate care grounds may have a positive effect on gonadotropin secretion even in the hypergonadotropic state as seen in Klinefelter syndrome ( ). Theoretically, this may result in higher levels of intra-testicular as well as circulating testosterone and maintained (or even augmented) spermatogenesis. However, no controlled trials are available and evidence is poor ( ). Hence, such therapies cannot be recommended in general. No data have been published on the possible positive or negative effects of testosterone treatment in boys with Klinefelter syndrome and compensated hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. The guideline group acknowledges that different strategies are employed. Some suggest that in the absence of clinical signs and symptoms of hypogonadism, these boys should not be treated with testosterone ( ). In some earlier studies, no benefit of TRT was observed in preventing obesity/overweight ( ), and no significant differences in bone structure or bone biomarkers were reported in patients with Klinefelter with and without testosterone therapy ( ). However, a recent study advocates testosterone treatment in cases with elevated LH in order to potentially positively affect the muscle mass, the BMD and neuropsychological functioning ( ). In young adults with Klinefelter syndrome, a recent placebo-controlled, randomised trial has shown that 6 months of testosterone treatment led to decreased total body and abdominal fat mass, as well as expected increases in haemoglobin and IGF-I ( ). In adults, individualised transdermal and injection testosterone therapy resulted in comparable treatment efficacy when evaluating androgen-responsive parameters ( ). There are now more than 1000 mutations reported ( ), and the genotype–phenotype correlation is highly variable. The estimated prevalence is 1–5 per 100 000 births ( , ). The phenotype depends on the residual AR function. According to the residual sensitivity to testosterone, the external genitalia will be variably virilised ( , , ). Androgen insensitivity syndrome (PAIS and CAIS) Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is a rare inherited condition caused by X-linked pathogenic mutations in the androgen receptor ( AR ) gene ( , ). There are now more than 1000 mutations reported ( ), and the genotype–phenotype correlation is highly variable. The estimated prevalence is 1–5 per 100 000 births ( , ). The phenotype depends on the residual AR function. According to the residual sensitivity to testosterone, the external genitalia will be variably virilised ( , , ). In general, three subgroups of AIS are defined. A complete absence of androgen receptor action leads to the clinical picture of CAIS. In these girls, the external genitalia are typically female. They have testes, which secrete testosterone with no (or markedly diminished) effect on the androgen receptor and Sertoli cells that produce AMH resulting in the regression of Mullerian structures prenatally. Thus, the uterus, fallopian tubes and upper part of the vagina are absent. Furthermore, Wolffian structures do not develop due to the insensitivity to testosterone. The testes are typically located within the abdomen, inguinal canal or in the labia majora ( ). Girls and women present during puberty with absence of menarche but with normal breast development due to the presence of androgens which are aromatised to oestrogens. Some girls (up to 50%) present with a bilateral inguinal hernia during infancy/childhood ( , , ). Women with CAIS do not develop pubic and axillary hair. A blind-ending vagina is observed in almost all patients (from 2.5 to 8 cm long). Women with CAIS have a female gender identity and are female in their gender role behaviour ( , ). Reduced AR residual activity results in PAIS with variable virilisation of the external genitalia during fetal life. Individuals generally present with ambiguous genitalia at birth. Earlier studies described a grading scheme (grade 1–5) for the description of virilisation ( ). The residual activity of the AR also leads to a variable degree of virilisation of the external genitalia and the presence of gynaecomastia at the onset of puberty. Unfortunately, the phenotype–genotype correlation is poor ( ). However, it has been shown that the degree of virilisation at birth estimated by the external masculinisation score (EMS) is a good predictor of the degree of virilisation at puberty ( , , ). In only 22% of the cases with a clinical diagnosis of PAIS, a pathogenic variant in the AR is found, making it a more complex and a highly variable clinical and diagnostic challenge ( , ). The mildest form of androgen insensitivity called mild androgen insensitivity syndrome is typically diagnosed in men with infertility without atypical genitalia ( , , ). A detailed description of this form is outside the scope of this guideline. Gonadectomy in patients with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome Patients with CAIS and intraabdominal testes might be at increased risk of developing gonadal germ cell cancers (GGCC), mainly seminomas, but this risk seems to be low before/during puberty ( , , ). Historically, nearly all patients with CAIS underwent gonadectomy before puberty because of this risk. Delaying gonadectomy allows for spontaneous pubertal development which is thought to be more satisfactory to the individual and also allows the patient to be fully involved in the shared decision-making to remove their gonads or not. There is an ongoing debate about the need to perform gonadectomy after puberty since the risk of invasive GGCC development is still uncertain. In a recent publication by Tack et al., an algorithm was presented, in which they suggest performing gonadectomy after puberty in individuals with CAIS and only after careful counselling. Yearly follow-up if the gonads are retained was advised including self-examination and imaging (ultrasound/MRI) ( ). However, self-examination is only possible when the gonads are located in the inguinal region. Women with CAIS and intact gonads have an increased risk of developing low BMD due to bone insensitivity to testosterone and relative oestrogen deficiency. After gonadectomy, the risk of developing low BMD further increases. Treatment with sex steroids aims to prevent osteoporosis and other metabolic complications ( , , , , , , ). Effects on cardiovascular health, quality of life, sexual health and mortality are less well studied ( , ). Pubertal induction in CAIS In whom to consider puberty induction? R 6.1 We recommend allowing girls with CAIS and retain gonads to go through spontaneous puberty. Rationale Puberty treatment is not indicated in girls with retained testes. In subjects with CAIS, androgen-responsive tissues including the pituitary gland are insensitive to testosterone, resulting in persistently elevated LH concentrations. Testosterone levels are within or above the normal male range in patients with retained testes. Testosterone is peripherally aromatised to oestrogen resulting in endogenous oestrogen levels which are above the male range but

health and mortality are less well studied ( , ). Pubertal induction in CAIS In whom to consider puberty induction? R 6.1 We recommend allowing girls with CAIS and retain gonads to go through spontaneous puberty. Rationale Puberty treatment is not indicated in girls with retained testes. In subjects with CAIS, androgen-responsive tissues including the pituitary gland are insensitive to testosterone, resulting in persistently elevated LH concentrations. Testosterone levels are within or above the normal male range in patients with retained testes. Testosterone is peripherally aromatised to oestrogen resulting in endogenous oestrogen levels which are above the male range but generally lower than the normal female range ( , ). These oestrogens induce breast development during puberty. In addition, this endogenous oestradiol has positive effects on the skeleton, brain and body habitus in patients with CAIS ( ). The patients develop no or scarce pubic and axillary hair. It is generally perceived that in patients with CAIS and intact gonads, spontaneous puberty occurs at the same age as described in the general population although one study reported the start of breast development at a median age of 12–13 years ( ). Furthermore, in patients with CAIS, final height is generally above the mean female final height but below the average height of the male population ( , , ). In individuals with intact gonads, oestrogen treatment can be considered in those with delayed puberty, particularly in individuals with tall stature with the aim to reduce final height. It is known that high dosages of oestrogens used during puberty can be successfully used to reduce final height in girls with constitutional tall stature ( , ). However, there are no studies reporting the effect of oestrogen treatment (dosage and timing) on the final height in patients with CAIS. Timing of puberty induction, treatment approach and monitoring R. 6.2 We recommend to start puberty induction at the age of 11 years in girls with CAIS who underwent gonadectomy. We recommend the same treatment protocols (for pubertal induction in girls with CAIS who have been gonadectomised ) as for other girls (R2.2–2.3, R2.6–2.8, R2.11). (+OOO) Rationale In girls with CAIS who have been gonadectomised, pubertal induction should start at the age of 11 years in accordance with the current treatment recommendations to mimic normal pubertal development. Treatment with sex hormones in patients with CAIS is generally only indicated when the gonads have been removed. The timing of puberty should be similar to other indications for pubertal induction in girls. Patients with CAIS treated with transdermal oestrogens were reported to have better bone health than those treated with oral formulations ( ). The risks and benefits of oral vs transdermal E2 are likely to be similar to other cohorts in whom these therapies have been studied more comprehensively, with regard to liver and cardiovascular adverse effects ( ). However, the benefits and disadvantages with regard to bone health and sexual function may differ for patients with other diagnoses. There are still conflicting data concerning the optimal dose of hormonal replacement therapy following puberty induction. Plasma oestradiol levels are positively associated with BMD. Therefore, routine monitoring of oestrogen concentrations by LC-MS/MS and bone density is recommended. Because of the absence of a uterus, the addition of treatment with progestins is generally not required. There is not enough evidence for a beneficial effect on brain, bone or other tissues to recommend the addition of progestin treatment. The use of testosterone rather than oestrogens in an attempt to mimic the hormonal levels of women with CAIS and intact gonads has been studied, particularly with regard to sexual function ( , , ). An unsolved aspect of the clinical care of young adults with CAIS and intact gonads is that although estrogen treatment is generally not recommended, low E2 plasma levels and BMD can be seen and thus, there may be a need for E2 or testosterone supplementation in these patients ( ). R 6.3 We recommend treatment monitoring every 3–6 months during puberty induction. Rationale Regular follow-up with clinical parameters (breast development, height), patient’s satisfaction and bone density. We suggest yearly measurements of FSH and LH as well as E2 levels similarly to (R2). Pubertal induction in PAIS In whom to consider puberty induction? R. 7.1 We recommend that in all patients with PAIS, evaluation of gender identity should take place before considering puberty induction. Rationale The clinical picture of PAIS is variable and depends on the residual androgen receptor activity and other modifying partially unknown factors. The genital phenotype ranges from hypospadias to female appearance ( ) ( ). Furthermore, the degree of virilisation at birth estimated by the EMS has been shown to be a good predictor of virilisation at puberty ( , , ). The external genitalia score (EGS) developed for evaluation in a

PAIS In whom to consider puberty induction? R. 7.1 We recommend that in all patients with PAIS, evaluation of gender identity should take place before considering puberty induction. Rationale The clinical picture of PAIS is variable and depends on the residual androgen receptor activity and other modifying partially unknown factors. The genital phenotype ranges from hypospadias to female appearance ( ) ( ). Furthermore, the degree of virilisation at birth estimated by the EMS has been shown to be a good predictor of virilisation at puberty ( , , ). The external genitalia score (EGS) developed for evaluation in a wider spectrum of genital differences may be used in the future ( ). Careful counselling by a multidisciplinary team is therefore required before any decision about hormonal treatment is taken. An experienced psychologist should evaluate the patients’ gender identity development, preferably from the age of 8 years. Structured psychological assessment of gender should be conducted. In case there are uncertainties about gender identity, puberty can be delayed by the use of GnRH agonists. Delay of puberty can be helpful in order to gain time to find out which gender will suit the individual best. Psychological follow-up is needed to evaluate gender development over time and keep an eye on the adolescent’s mental health (emotional problems such as social phobia or depression need to be identified and treated). Recognising that gender identity is a non-binary phenomenon can facilitate satisfaction with one’s gender. Detailed information is provided under ‘Psychological Aspects’. However, pubertal treatment is essential for long-term wellbeing in all patients, and a decision regarding hormonal treatment eventually has to be made. Evaluation of pubertal development R. 7.2 We recommend that careful evaluation of patients’ endocrine profile, phenotype and genotype is undertaken and that this information is used to consider the potential for virilisation during puberty (in patients with a male or undecided/binary identity). Rationale To evaluate the degree of pubertal development in PAIS, we recommend monitoring clinical signs of virilisation, height, full hormonal evaluation, degree of masculinisation at birth (EMS/EGS) and the genetic variant. At the onset of puberty, the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator initiates pulsatile GnRH secretion resulting in pulsatile FSH and LH secretion from the pituitary gland. The resulting testosterone secretion from the Leydig cells in the testes fails to exert negative feedback to the hypothalamic-pituitary axis due to insufficient central AR action. However, the increased circulating testosterone is aromatised to oestradiol which exerts normal negative feedback on FSH levels that typically remain within the normal range. Thus, the LH/FSH ratio is typically relatively high in CAIS and PAIS ( , ). Oestradiol circulates in high-normal concentrations (compared to the male reference range) resulting in gynaecomastia in many boys with PAIS ( , ). The testicular Sertoli cell markers inhibin B and AMH are within the normal prepubertal male range ( ). In the physiological situation, inhibin B increases with pubertal onset, whereas AMH decreases when the Sertoli cells differentiate and start to express AR. With rising intratesticular testosterone levels, AMH secretion is inhibited in a subject with normal AR function, whereas a boy with PAIS continues to have prepubertal levels of AMH due to lack of inhibition. Inhibin B is usually within normal male ranges in boys with PAIS ( ). It is difficult to predict the course of puberty in patients with PAIS. A study analysed EMS at birth in 27 PAIS patients in relation to the pubertal outcome and found that only six of nine patients with EMS < 5 at birth underwent spontaneous male onset of puberty, whereas all 18 patients with EMS ≥ 5 at birth experienced a spontaneous male onset of puberty. In contrast to the clinical findings, the functional analysis of AR variants did not appear to predict pubertal outcome ( ). It remains to be seen to which degree the early (peripubertal) changes in reproductive hormones will guide the clinician in the prediction of spontaneous virilisation. Treatment approach and monitoring R. 7.3 In children with PAIS identifying as as girls, the general recommendations for pubertal induction in CAIS as formulated under R 6.2–6.3 apply. Rationale In children with PAIS who have been raised as girls and identify as girls and who have not been gonadectomised, gonadectomy can be considered before or at the very beginning of puberty, to avoid virilisation and gender discomfort/dysphoria in addition to considerations regarding malignancy risk ( , , , , , ). Pubertal induction as recommended for other conditions in which pubertal induction is necessary applies. R 7.4 In boys with PAIS, we suggest considering additional testosterone treatment in mid puberty depending on the clinical and biochemical assessment of pubertal development. If clinical signs of hypoandrogenism such as micropenis and gynaecomastia are present, we suggest treating with the addition of testosterone for 6 months and then

have not been gonadectomised, gonadectomy can be considered before or at the very beginning of puberty, to avoid virilisation and gender discomfort/dysphoria in addition to considerations regarding malignancy risk ( , , , , , ). Pubertal induction as recommended for other conditions in which pubertal induction is necessary applies. R 7.4 In boys with PAIS, we suggest considering additional testosterone treatment in mid puberty depending on the clinical and biochemical assessment of pubertal development. If clinical signs of hypoandrogenism such as micropenis and gynaecomastia are present, we suggest treating with the addition of testosterone for 6 months and then evaluating the effect. (+OOO) Rationale The clinical phenotype of individuals with PAIS who identify as males is highly variable from micropenis to severe hypospadias and/or bifid scrotum. It is a theoretical consideration that the inherent androgen insensitivity can be overcome by adding supraphysiological testosterone levels on top of the endogenous testosterone secretion. Anecdotally, patients report a beneficial effect on genital growth and wellbeing, but no randomised trials exist. Transdermal testosterone and long-acting i.m. injections have been tried ( ). Clearly, serum testosterone concentrations cannot be used to monitor efficacy, which relies exclusively on clinical improvement and general wellbeing. Biochemically, haematocrit is suggested as a safety parameter. LH has also been suggested as a surrogate marker for optimal dosing of testosterone in males with PAIS. The majority of males with PAIS develop gynaecomastia ( , , ), which may theoretically either worsen (because of increased E2) or improve (because of lowered LH-induced aromatase activity) with pharmacological testosterone treatment ( ). Breast cancer has only been described in a few cases ( ). The effect of medical treatment on gynaecomastia is variable and most males decide to undergo mastectomy. Based on the beneficial effects of oestrogen receptor blocking in pubertal gynaecomastia, this treatment modality could also be considered in male patients with PAIS ( ). Successful use of tamoxifen, a selective oestrogen receptor blocker, to reduce gynaecomastia was described in two patients with PAIS ( ). However, long-term studies are lacking, and whether or not there is a role for oestrogen blockers to prevent gynecomastia remains to be studied. Other signs of under-virilisation in patients with PAIS raised as boys, such as hypospadias and cryptorchidism, have been surgically corrected during infancy or childhood in most patients. Future perspectives Most of the recommendations in this guideline are based on expert clinical experience and often a long-term clinical experience of treating a large number of individuals. Studies on pubertal induction specifically in individuals with a DSD are scarce. It is clear that further studies are needed. Just to mention a few, issues directly related to hormone treatment with improved formulations and optimal route of administration as well as timing and progression of puberty are needed. The function and importance of the mini-puberty are still largely unknown. The issue of fertility and how the possibility for future fertility can be improved for individuals with different diagnoses are attracting increased attention. Does the treatment with FSH and LH/hCG before the start of testosterone increase the possibility of future fertility in CHH? Studies on optimisation of sex hormone replacement in AIS and how to avoid long-term consequences for these patients are warranted. Animal studies and stem-cell research may open possibilities for the development of novel technologies involving Leydig cell transplantation in male hypogonadism in the future ( ). Diagnostic difficulties to distinguish CHH vs CDGP are still largely unsolved and a clinical recurrent issue. Improved tools for identifying a halt in pubertal development would be of benefit for many patients. Improved psychosocial support for patients is essential. Conclusion Disorders of sexual development comprise a large array of diagnoses and patients with CHH and DSD present different symptoms and needs, especially during puberty. The care for these individuals and their families needs to be individualised and requires the involvement of specialised multidisciplinary teams. chunks.content: Introduction Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) constitute the major cause of death in developed countries, representing 32% of annual deaths worldwide and involve high economic costs for public health systems (Available from, ). High low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDLc) plasma levels are associated with CVDs (Cholesterol-lowering bioactive foods & nutraceuticals in pediatrics: clinical evidence of efficacy & safety., ). Childhood is the optimal period for early hypercholesterolemia screening, since although cardiovascular events are not common in children, they may have morphological and functional modifications in the vessel wall, since the atherosclerotic process can start very early in life (Kusters Dorothé et al., ). Hypercholesterolemia is usually countered by a healthy lifestyle (diet and physical activity) and cholesterol-lowering medications that prevent eventual clinical complications associated with these diseases (Ademi et al., ). Due to the long-term efficacy and adverse events of pharmacological interventions, public health programs claim the importance of adopting healthy diets and lifestyle habits, mainly in children and young adults, committed to the improvement of plasma lipid profile, intending to delay pharmacological interventions and the onset of clinical complications (Kaminsky et al., ). Among different CVD-preventing interventions, a wide range of clinical trials highlight the effectiveness of the Mediterranean diet as a traditional balanced diet and lifestyle habits, in which extra-virgin olive oil (EVOO) plays a key role as the main culinary fat (Martínez-González et al., ). The health-enhancing properties of EVOO are attributed to the presence of several constituents, including unsaturated fatty acids, mostly represented by oleic acid, and other minor phytochemical constituents, such as polyphenols i.e., tyrosols, oleuropein, and other secoiridoids; tocopherols; triterpenoid acids, such as maslinic and oleanoic acids; and phytosterols such as campesterol, β-sitosterol, fucosterol, and stigmasterol (Paz et al., ). Phytosterols are considered efficient plant-derived hypocholesterolemic agents because of their structural similarity to cholesterol, which interferes with their absorption, biosynthesis, and metabolism in the human body. Therefore, they have recently been considered promising candidates for the treatment of hypercholesterolemia and associated complications in children (Wójcik, ). Lipidomics has emerged as a powerful tool to comprehensively characterize lipid profiles and to elucidate their roles in health and disease. In this framework, phytosterols are of particular interest, as their structural similarity to cholesterol allows them to modulate lipid metabolism and influence membrane dynamics. Integrating phytosterol research into lipidomics not only provides a deeper understanding of their biological functions but also opens avenues for identifying novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets related to metabolic disorders, cardiovascular health, and nutrition. The present interventional, crossover, clinical trial aimed to evaluate the effect of the daily intake of a spreadable cream based on EVOO enriched in phytosterols (PESC) for 8 weeks on children and adolescents with untreated hypercholesterolemia compared with the intake of a control EVOO-spreadable cream without phytosterols (CSC). Anthropometric and biochemical parameters related to cardiovascular risk and a lipidomics-based workflow, via liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS), were performed to decipher the effect of PESC administration at a lipid metabolome-wide level. Chemometric analyses and the application of multivariate statistics-based chemometric tests were used to better interpret the particular effects of either single or combined factors on the plasma lipid profile of children with hypercholesterolemia. Our data opens new perspectives for the management of hypercholesterolemia and paves the way for the design of novel functional food products. Methods Extra virgin olive oil-based phytosterols-enriched spreadable cream and control spreadable cream The PESC experimental spreadable cream, based on EVOO and enriched in phytosterols, and the CSC control cream were prepared in 15 g single-dose containers using a base of 90% EVOO. Each single dose of PESC preparation was added with 1.2 g of free phytosterols (Vegapure 95E, Reference: 30,534,530, CAS: 83-48-7, BASF Nutrition & Health, Germany), whereas the CSC was the same EVOO-spreadable cream without phytosterols. The experimental dose of phytosterols was adjusted in compliance with the European regulation 2000/500/CE, which sets a maximum daily amount of 3 g/day of free plant sterols, which represents 8% of free phytosterols in the experimental spreadable cream. The EVOO-spreadable creams were prepared in ACER CAMPESTRES S.L. Table shows the chemical compositions of the two spreadable creams. Phytosterols were analyzed using gas chromatography at the Instituto de la Grasa (CSIC, Sevilla), as previously described (García-González et al., ). Considering an average weight of approximately 20 kg for 6-year-old children, 40 kg for 12-year-old and 60 kg for 16-year-old, the doses of plant sterols were adjusted for weight ranges. Children weighing > 20 kg and < 40 kg received a single daily 15-g dose of spreadable cream (0.03–0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day), whereas children weighing ≥ 40 kg and up to 60 kg received two 15-g doses per day (0.04–0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day). Since both PESC and CSC were EVOO-based, participation in this study did not entail any potential risks. Experimental design A

). Considering an average weight of approximately 20 kg for 6-year-old children, 40 kg for 12-year-old and 60 kg for 16-year-old, the doses of plant sterols were adjusted for weight ranges. Children weighing > 20 kg and < 40 kg received a single daily 15-g dose of spreadable cream (0.03–0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day), whereas children weighing ≥ 40 kg and up to 60 kg received two 15-g doses per day (0.04–0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day). Since both PESC and CSC were EVOO-based, participation in this study did not entail any potential risks. Experimental design A randomized, double-blind, crossover, controlled trial was conducted in the Reina Sofía University Hospital of Córdoba (Spain), comprising the daily consumption of PESC compared with the control CSC creams. The intervention was conducted for 5 months divided into two periods of 8 weeks separated by a wash-out period of 4 weeks, after which crossover was carried out. Allocation into the two sequences of spread cream administration was performed using a stratified block randomization method adjusted for age and sex. The randomization list was concealed in a light-proof sealed envelope. The sealed envelope was maintained by an independent statistician. Therefore, the children and researchers were blinded to treatment allocation throughout the study. Blood pressure, body mass index, and blood sampling were performed before and after the two 8-week intervention periods (t1 and t2). The participants were instructed to return the individual spreadable containers that were not consumed during each intervention period for compliance determination. Intervention compliance was calculated as a percentage by dividing the dosages consumed by those indicated for the entire period of intervention. The protocol was conducted following the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines (Vijayananthan & Nawawi, ; World Medical Association, ). All investigators were qualified to conduct and supervise the trial. The parents or tutors of the participants provided written informed consent before study entry. The sample size was calculated assuming a decrease in total cholesterol of 10%, an alpha error of 0.05, a type-2 Beta error of 0.2, and a loss of children of 15% throughout the study, indicating 25 children for each group were required. The clinical trial protocol has been registered previously in: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05460208 . Participants and eligibility Fifty-six children and adolescents (33 boys and 23 girls) were recruited from the pediatric Clinical Management Unit of the Reina Sofía University Hospital in Córdoba (Spain). The inclusion criteria were as follows: children between 6 and 18 years old who agreed to participate in the study and whose parents were willing to provide written informed consent for adherence to the protocol, diagnosed with hypercholesterolemia, and not receiving any treatment for hypercholesterolemia or any other pathology. The exclusion criteria were as follows: intake of hypocholesterolemic drugs or any other drug, suffering from other metabolic diseases, and unwillingness to sign the informed consent. Six children did not meet the inclusion criteria, and only 50 children were finally included (30 boys and 20 girls). Children were randomly divided into two groups. Daily, children allocated to group A (n = 24; 13 boys and 11 girls) received the corresponding dose of the control CSC (depending on their body weight, as described above) for 8 weeks, whereas children in group B (n = 26; 17 boys and 9 girls) received the corresponding dose of the enriched PESC during the same period. Eight weeks after the administration of the spreadable cream, it was interrupted, and a wash-out period of 4 weeks was initiated. One boy and two girls from group A dropped out during the first period of intervention because they did not like the spread texture. Afterward, a crossover for both groups was implemented, and children in group A (n = 21; 12 boys and 9 girls) took the PESC cream, while those in group B (n = 26; 17 boys and 9 girls) took the CSC cream during the following 8 weeks. During the second intervention period, one boy from group B and three girls from group A dropped out because they did not want to be drawn again. Thus, only 18 children (12 boys and 6 girls) from Group A and 25 children (16 boys and 9 girls) from Group B remained in the study at the end of the intervention. Additionally, to find a reliable effect of phytosterol intake, we calculated adherence to the intervention compliance and for statistical data analysis we established a cut-off value to select those samples from subjects presenting at least 70% of treatment adherence. Thus, 10 and 13 children were included in groups A and B, respectively, for metabolomic data analyses. A flowchart of the study is shown in Fig. . Clinical and biochemical parameters Body weight and height were measured using standardized procedures. Body mass index (BMI, kg/m 2 ) and BMI z score were calculated for all participants using the standard growth percentile charts for the Spanish population (Begoña et al., ). Overweight and obesity were defined as BMI z scores ≥ 1 and ≥ 2, respectively, in participants under 18 years old and BMI > 25 and 30 kg/m 2 in those older than 18 years and children are classified as underweight if their BMI z score ≤ -2 according to the WHO guidelines (World Health Organization, ). Systolic and diastolic blood pressures (mmHg) and heart rate were measured with a mercury sphygmomanometer (Dinamap V-100) after a minimum of 10 min of rest in the seated position, and the average of two measurements was recorded before and after each intervention period. Additionally, after a 12 h overnight fasting period, blood samples were taken at time points t1 and t2 (basal and after 8 weeks of intervention, respectively) of both periods to perform biochemical and metabolomics analyses. Serum and plasma were obtained by centrifugation in tubes containing a gel separator (for serum) and EDTA (for plasma) for 10 min at 3700 rpm and 4 °C. Aliquots of serum and plasma were stored at −80 °C for specific analysis. The primary outcomes were total cholesterol (TC) and LDLc serum concentrations. TC, LDLc, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDLc), triacylglycerols (TAG), glucose, urea, creatinine, uric acid, bilirubin, total proteins, ferritin, transferrin concentrations, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) activity were analyzed in serum using standardized clinical methods with Architect c16000 and i2000SR autoanalyzers (Abbott Diagnostics®, Abbot Laboratories, Madrid, Spain). Insulin was analyzed using chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays. All parameters were analyzed at the Clinical Analysis Laboratory of the Reina Sofia University Hospital. External and internal quality controls were performed according to the hospital protocols. Sample preparation for lipidomic analysis Plasma lipidomic analysis was performed as a secondary outcome. Plasma aliquots samples were thawed and stored at 4 °C until analysis, and 200 μL was mixed with 800 μL of a cold methanol/acetonitrile (1/1, v/v ) solution, vortexed for 30 s, and then subjected to ultrasound-assisted extraction for 10 min. Next, 10 μL of 1% formic acid ( v / v ) was added and incubated at −18 ℃ overnight to allow for protein precipitation. The samples were then centrifuged for 15 min at 17,000 rpm and 4 °C. Finally, the supernatants were filtered into analytical vials using 0.22-micron cellulose syringe filters. Quality control (QC) was performed by mixing a small aliquot of each sample (10 μL) into the same vial. Untargeted UHPLC-Orbitrap-MS lipidomics analysis of plasma samples. The untargeted lipidomic profiling of each sample was performed using a Q Exactive™ Focus Hybrid Quadrupole-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) coupled to a Vanquish ultra-high-pressure liquid chromatography (UHPLC) pump and equipped with a HESI-II probe (Thermo Scientific, USA). The chromatographic separation was performed using a BEH C18 (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 µm) column maintained at 40 °C. The mobile phase consisted of 5 mM ammonium formate and 0.1% formic acid in water/methanol (95/5, v/v; solution A) and 5 mM ammonium formate and 0.1% formic acid in 2-propanol/methanol/water (65/30/5, v/v/v; solution B). The automatic gain control target (AGC target) was 106, and the maximum injection time (IT) was 100 ms. The injection volume was 5 µL and the m/z range for the full scan analysis was 150–1500 m/z. The Top N ions were selected for further fragmentation (data-dependent MS/MS workflow) under stepped normalized collision energies (10, 20, and 40 eV). The parameters of the heated electrospray ionization (HESI) were spray voltage 3.5 kV for HESI + and 2.8 kV for HESI-, capillary temperature 320 °C, sheath gas flow 30 arbitrary units (arb) and auxiliary gas flow 10 arb. The mass spectrometer was calibrated using positive and negative ion calibration solutions (Pierce™; Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA, USA). To avoid possible bias, the injection sequence was randomized. The collected RAW files were further processed using two open-source software packages, MS-DIAL (version 4.70) (Hiroshi et al., ) and MS-Finder (Hiroshi et al., ). Therefore, automatic peak finding, LOWESS normalization, and spectral matching annotation against the LipidBLAST database were performed. For peaks with a minimum peak height of 10,000 cps for HESI + and HESI- polarities, a mass range of 100–1500 m/z was inspected. In addition, the MS tolerances for peak centroiding were 0.01 Da and 0.05 Da for MS/MS. The identification step (set > 50% for annotation) was based on mass accuracy, isotopic pattern, and spectral matching, considering the usual ion adducts for lipidomics. To fill in missing peaks, gap-filling based on the peak finder algorithm was used considering a 5-ppm tolerance for m/z values. To conclude, using an identification score > 5, in in-silico fragmentation of the not fully annotated MS/MS features was achieved using MS-Finder software, considering the available database (i.e., Lipid Maps). Chemometrics analyses, data processing and statistics The experimental design included three factors: group (A or B), treatment (PESC for the experimental group, and CSC for the control group), and sampling time (before and after the intervention, t1 and t2, respectively). Lipidomics results were thoroughly processed using different chemometric analyses. First, to determine the influence of each factor on the lipid profile of plasma samples, unsupervised hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) was performed using Mass Profiler Professional software (Agilent Technologies®, Santa Clara, CA, USA), as previously described (El-Nakhel et al., ). For this purpose, the abundance of annotated features was subjected to log 2 transformation, normalization at the 75th percentile, and baselining against the median value of all samples. The resulting hierarchical cluster was obtained based on a fold-change-based heatmap and combined with a dendrogram built on Euclidean distances by applying the Ward’s linkage rule. Additionally, a supervised multivariate analysis based on the analysis of variance (ANOVA) multi-block orthogonal partial least squares (AMOPLS) was performed using the “rAMOPLS” package (version 0.2) in the R software (version 4.2.3), as previously described (Boccard et al., ). For this purpose, log 2 -transformed abundances of annotated features were subjected to AMOPLS modeling to determine the ANOVA-mediated discriminant power of each factor: “treatment”, “time”, and “group” as described above, as well as their interactions. Models were built by performing 100 permutations, and 10-step stratified sub-sampling was carried out to cope with the sample population differences between groups due to the unbalanced experimental design. The results for the modeling were obtained by optimizing the smallest number of orthogonal components showing statistical significance ( α = 0.01). The model interpretation was based on the relative sum of squares (RSS), which indicates the reliability of observed effects by reflecting the proportion (in percentage) of the variability attributed to each factor; residual structure ratio (RSR), which represents the ANOVA consistency of each effect concerning residuals, assuming that the highest values correlate with the highest contribution of each effect; p -value, which represents the statistical significance of each effect; principal predictive components (in percentage), which represent the major block contributions associated with each effect; and orthogonal component (in percentage), which represents the contribution of the orthogonal predictive component. Additionally, AMOPLS models were analyzed based on the variable importance in the projection (VIP), represented by VIP 2 markers, corresponding to the metabolites showing the strongest discriminating influence for each factor. The top-20 VIP 2 markers exhibiting the highest score were selected and combined with their logarithm of fold change values (logFC) and probability values to achieve pairwise comparisons by volcano analysis. Baseline anthropometric, clinical and biochemical parameters were statistically analyzed by T test and χ 2 test for quantitative and qualitative variables, respectively, after checking normality of variables and homogeneity of variance to compare the two groups of intervention. Non-normal variables were log transformed and used for analysis. Finally, the results after the intervention from anthropometric, clinical, and biochemical parameters were statistically

Results Basal description of volunteers included in the study Table describes the anthropometric, clinical, and serum biochemical parameters of 23 children who met ≥ 70% compliance included in group A (starting with CSC) and group B (starting with PESC) before the beginning of the intervention. No statistical differences were observed in these values, except for serum HDLc serum levels, which were higher in group A than in the children included in group B. At baseline, 74% of children were normal-weight, 12% were overweight and 14% were obese children. Clinical and biochemical parameters of selected volunteers included in lipidomic analysis After selecting volunteers who complied with more than 70% adherence to the treatment (n = 10 for group A and n = 13 for group B), we found significant differences in the baseline for HDLc and ALP (Table ). Similarly, we found differences between groups for HDLc, ALP and uric acid, as well as SBP (“Group × Treatment”) and LDLc (“Group × Treatment” and “Group × Time”) (Supplementary Table ). Serum TC and LDLc levels were affected differently by the treatments, with significantly lower concentrations in the PESC-treated samples: 11.3%, p < 0.01, and 17.2%, p < 0.001 for TC and LDLc, respectively, compared to the control (Fig. and Supplementary Table ). In addition, when evaluating the “Time × Treatment” effect, we found that both TC and LDLc serum levels significantly decreased ( p = 0.050 and p = 0.022, respectively) in volunteers after the intake of either PESC or CSC (Fig. ). No significant effects were found on the rest of the anthropometric, blood pressure, and biochemical parameters due to the intake of any spreadable creams (Supplementary Table ). Lipidomics combined with chemometrics analysis reveals the effect of PESC on plasmatic lipid profile The results from the plasma lipidomic profile of subjects involved in the present clinical trial showed a total of 1,948 features effectively annotated using the database LipidBlast for all samples, from which 455 metabolites were annotated at the MS 2 level (165 annotated in silico) and the rest were annotated at the MS-only level. For each annotated feature, the name, annotation level, average retention time (min), average mass (u), related adducts, molecular formula, ontology, International Chemical Identifier (InChiKey), simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES), annotation score, MS isotopic spectrum, MS 2 spectrum, and raw abundance values are listed in Supplementary Table . A wide variety of lipids have been reported in plasma samples, including acylcarnitines, N-acyl amino acids, sulfolipids, glycerolipids, mostly diacylglycerols (DAGs) and TAGs, and a heterogeneous range of phospholipids, lysophospholipids, and sphingolipids, mostly represented by ceramides and sphingomyelins (Supplementary Table ). Moreover, sterol derivatives were also reported in all samples, including cholic acids, vitamin A and D esters, fatty acid esters, and acylhexosyl derivatives of plant sterols, as shown for brassicasterol, campesterol, and sitosterol, whose levels were constant in all samples. The results from the AMOPLS modeling considering all factors are displayed in Table and Fig. . Data indicate that three factors were found to be statistically significant: “Time” and the interactions “Group x Treatment,” and “Time x Treatment” ( p < 0.05; Table ). To gain insight into the influence of each factor, the RSS and RSR reveal that the interaction "Group x Treatment" contributes with a 14.8% in explaining the variability reported by the model as well as provides the highest RSR value (1.47), whereas “Time” represents 9.0%, and the rest of the factors exhibit a marginal contribution (RSS < 2%). In addition, treatment played a significant role in the interaction with time, reporting an RSS of 1.2% for the factor “Time x Treatment.” Moreover, a high contribution associated with the residuals (RSS = 70.9%) was observed, suggesting the significant involvement of additional non-considered factors in the modulation of the lipidomics plasma profile (Table ). The most important variables in the projection of the AMOPLS model were represented by VIP 2 metabolite markers, which were specifically obtained for the interaction between “Time x Treatment”, indicating their influence in the projection and the calculated logFC and statistical probability, according to t -test analysis for each pairwise comparison (Table ). The identified VIP 2 markers included a large proportion (20%) of phospholipids and lysophospholipids, showing an accumulation of phospholipids for PESC at t2 (logFC = 0.20–1.58), with PE P-15:2/17:4 being significantly accumulated ( p < 0.05), whereas the lysophospholipid LPC 9:0 accumulated in CSC at t2 (logFC = −0.31). Furthermore, VIP 2 markers also showed a large proportion of sphingolipids, characterized by a non-significant accumulation of phytosphingosines (logFC = 0.20–1.58) reported for PESC at t2 with respect to CSC, combined with a downregulation of the sphinganine SPB 26:0;2O (log FC = −0.22). At the same time, PESC promoted the accumulation of DAG at t2 with respect to the control (logFC = 0.12–1.26), and DAG 33:6 showed a significant accumulation ( p < 0.05). Concerning the EVOO phytoconstituents, PESC promoted a slight accumulation of sitosterol (ST29:1;O, logFC = 0.02), as well as vitamin A fatty acid esters (VAEs) (logFC = 0.32–0.41), which was statistically significant in the case of VAE 6:0 ( p < 0.05). Discussion The present study has demonstrated that daily supplementation with 0.03 – 0.06 g plant sterols/kg of body weight/day provided into an EVOO-based spreadable cream for 8 weeks may decrease serum cholesterol (TC and LDLc) and modify lipidic metabolites in children with untreated hypercholesterolemia. Phytosterols can be used as an important tool for the primary prevention of hypercholesterolemia and may also contribute to the prevention of cardiovascular events in patients with high-to-moderate serum levels of LDLc (Fontané et al., ; Gao et al., ; Wang et al., ). However, for severe hypercholesterolemia and familial hypercholesterolemia, it is necessary to combine dietary treatment with pharmacological treatment mainly statins (Turini et al., ). Pharmacotherapy in children and adolescents is only recommended from the age of 10 years when they do not respond positively to lifestyle modifications, particularly for those with LDLc serum levels ≥ 190 mg/dL (Jellinger et al., ). Previously, a daily intake of 2–3 g of phytosterols has been demonstrated to reduce LDLc levels by approximately 10–15% in adults (Musa-Veloso et al., ; Ruuth et al., ). In accordance with our results, an umbrella meta-analysis has confirmed that the daily administration of phytosterol in adults significantly reduces LDLc and TC, mainly at doses of ≥ 2 g/day and treatment duration > 8 weeks, suggesting its possible application as a complementary therapy for cardiovascular risk reduction (Wang et al., ). These authors also described a lower but significant beneficial effect on serum TAG that we did not find in our volunteers, probably because of the low levels found in the children included in the present study (Simin et al., ). On the other hand, another recent umbrella review based in meta-analyses has confirmed the LDLc-lowering effects of phytosterols but not the effect on plasma TAG and HDLc concentrations in adults, and highlight the need for long-term follow-up, well-designed clinical trials with large sample size to demonstrate the benefits of phytosterols on health (Liu et al., ). Although our results corroborate the efficient plasma cholesterol-lowering effect of plant phytosterols, we did not find a significant accumulation of esters and acylhexosyl-derivatives. It is worth highlighting that these compounds were solely annotated based on their ms1, which raises the possibility of incorrect assignments. Nonetheless, sitosterol, annotated at ms2 level, was found in the plasma of children treated with the phytosterol-enriched cream. This fact is probably because the main mechanism of action of phytosterols is intestinal competition with cholesterol for micellization, transport, and absorption (Li et al., ), and they scarcely reach the bloodstream. Borel reported that the effectiveness of the absorption of sitosterol and campesterol is approximately 0.51–1.9% (Borel, ), and Li et al. agreed that the intestinal absorption rate of phytosterols is less than 5%, much lower than that of cholesterol (50–60%), and depends on many genetic, physiological, and nutritional factors (Li et al., ). In fact, some authors have suggested that the hypocholesterolemic effect of phytosterols may be mediated by changing the structure of the gastrointestinal microbiota (Lv et al., ). One limitation of the present study is that we have not analyzed microbiota changes induced by the intake of the phytosterol-enriched cream, nor metabolites derived from its metabolism. Therefore, more studies are needed to identify these potential microbiota-derived hypocholesterolemic mechanisms. Given the complexity of the lipid profile provided by the lipidomics approach, the application of multivariate chemometrics analyses is essential to determine the biological significance of annotated metabolites and to better interpret the effect of phytosterol intake on lipid metabolism modulation in the children included in the present study. Thus, the experimental design included three factors: Group (A or B), Treatment (PESC or CSC), and sampling Time (before and after the intervention, t1 and t2, respectively), which were expected to intricately influence the lipid profile in a complex manner. The results derived from HCA support the complex interaction between all the factors involved in this study, as well as the interactions that could eventually occur among them. This evidence was mainly supported by the supervised AMOPLS model, which showed that treatment played a significant role in the plasma lipidomic profile in the interactions “Group x Treatment” and “Time x Treatment”. Indeed, the results from AMOPLS modeling show differences associated with the intervention groups (A or B), which is in line with the differences observed in the biochemical parameters abovementioned, including differences in HDLc and LDLc. In fact, it has been shown that HDL and LDL cholesterol contain their own lipidome (Kontush et al., ) predominantly constituted by several species of lysophosphatidilcholine, phosphatidylcholyne, and phosphatidylethanolamine among others. Lipids corresponding to such classes were among the top metabolites in the Group x Treatment interaction (Table ). One of the main strengths of AMOPLS is that it has individual predictive components, each focused on a specific effect or interaction. As a result, regardless of the variability explained by each factor or the significance of other factors, it allows for the independent biological interpretation of each independent factor. Therefore, we extracted that the main discriminant metabolites associated with the interaction “Time x Treatment” were phospholipids and lysophospholipids (20%), sphingolipids (20%), as well as DAGs and VAEs. The results showed the accumulation of phospholipids, phytosphingosines, DAGs, and VAEs at the end of the intervention in the PESC-treated compared with the control group. This modulation provided by PESC at the end of the intervention involves phospholipids and DAGs, two of the major constituents of lipoproteins, as well as sphingolipids, which participate in the recognition of their cell receptors (Mikhailova et al., ). These findings suggest the regulation of lipoprotein metabolism by PESC by interfering with their assembly and mobilization and may also be implicated in the previously described better functionality of HDLc induced by phytosterols that may contribute to the cholesterol efflux and therefore for plasma cholesterol reduction (Soltani Saba et al., ). Indeed, our lipidomic results are barely significant and should motivate further research to link the plasma lipidomic profile with the observed biochemical parameters involved in the evaluation of hypercholesterolemia. To the best of our knowledge, no other study has investigated changes in lipid metabolites in humans, either children or adults, with hypercholesterolemia after supplementation with plant phytosterols.
